title: Facets of two-dimensional infinite group problems
contribution: Lays the foundation for the two-dimensional mixed integer infinite group problem: finite tools to verify subadditivity and facetness, the first two facet families (row aggregation of 1D facets, which captures every two-gradient PL facet, and a three-gradient family whose continuous coefficients are not dominated by single-row GMICs).
problem_entry: Commercial cuts come from single rows; multi-row group relaxations should represent continuous variables better, and Dash-Gunluk computations show weak continuous coefficients in 1D group cuts (pp. 1-2); no facets of 2DMIIGP were known (abstract p. 1).
key_idea: Finite subadditivity checks at boundary points (Props. 6, 10, 12, pp. 6-11), a 2D set-sum analogue of the Interval Lemma (Prop. 24, pp. 13-14), aggregation construction kappa(x,y)=zeta((x+y) mod 1) (Construction 31/38, pp. 16-20) and a three-gradient construction (Construction 44, pp. 22-23).
assumptions: Infinite group I^2 with finite-support solutions (Def. 1, p. 3); continuous piecewise-linear functions (pp. 5-6); Johnson's limit formula for continuous coefficients (Theorem 51, p. 29); f1, f2 nonzero for the three-gradient family (p. 22).
proof_devices: subadditivity of a PL function reduced to finitely many inequalities at boundary points and supplemental vertices (Prop. 6 p. 6, Props. 10 and 12 pp. 7, 11)
2D set-sum interval lemma without continuity, applied region by region to show uniqueness of E(phi) (Prop. 24 pp. 13-14; Theorem 48 p. 28)
Facet Theorem route: minimality plus unique solution of the equality system (Theorem 17, p. 12)
two-gradient characterisation: no vertices, parallel edges, edge through origin, reduction to Construction 38 (Theorem 42, pp. 21-22)
GMIC has strongest continuous coefficients among 1D facets via subadditivity contradiction (Prop. 54, p. 30)
experiments: none; one two-variable IP example where the three-gradient cut is facet-defining and both single-row GMICs are not (Example 55, p. 31).
positioning: Extends Gomory-Johnson's 1D infinite group theory and Johnson's general results to two rows; motivated by Dash-Gunluk computational findings (pp. 2, 4).
writing: Section-by-section roadmap naming each key proposition/theorem in the introduction (p. 2); conclusion restates results and lists three numbered future directions (pp. 31-32).
limits_future: No computational test; future: evaluation in branch-and-cut, more 2DMIIGP facets, extension to n-dimensional groups (p. 32).

method_links.note: Pre-2019 stance: single-row cuts are the limit to go beyond via multi-row relaxations, still MILP-internal.
Completeness theorem bounds Construction 38 (all two-gradient PL facets) and a second family is shown outside it.
Claims the aggregation family explains the success of constraint aggregation in practice, without measuring practice.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Subadditivity of PL functions on the infinite group I^2 reduced to finitely many point inequalities.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: compose low-dimensional facets into high-dimensional ones
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Facets of 2DIIGP from 1D facets by row aggregation and homomorphisms.

transferable: Prove subadditivity of a piecewise-linear function by checking pairs of breakpoints/vertices only, adding supplemental vertices where needed (Prop. 6, p. 6; Prop. 32 proof, p. 17).
Replace a 1D uniqueness lemma by a set-sum (U+V) version without continuity and apply it to adjacent regions (Prop. 24, pp. 13-14; Theorem 48, p. 28).
End a theory paper with a tiny IP where the new cut is facet-defining and classical cuts are not (Example 55, p. 31).

quotes.text: Proving that a subadditive function φ is facet-defining is typically difficult.
This method requires the verification of subadditivity of the function at a finite number of carefully selected points.

title: Linear-programming-based lifting and its application to primal cutting-plane algorithms
contribution: Proposes an approximate multi-constraint lifting procedure that needs one LP per coefficient, uses it to strengthen Gomory fractional cuts inside Glover's primal algorithm with finite convergence, and shows the modified algorithm beats Glover's algorithm and the best published primal results on knapsack and small MIPLIB instances.
problem_entry: Primal cutting-plane algorithms keep an integer feasible solution and allow re-optimisation but have been dormant since the 1970s and need strong cuts; lifting for unstructured multi-constraint IPs is hard (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Relax integrality of all variables except the one being lifted so each lifting bound is an LP (eqs. (7)-(8), p. 5); fixing at a bound yields an integral coefficient from one LP (Corollary 8, p. 10); apply to Gomory fractional cuts in Glover's algorithm (pp. 12-13).
assumptions: Pure IP with rational data, Ax <= b, x in Z+ (p. 4); integral cut coefficients and rhs assumed for simplicity (p. 4); Glover special row (pp. 12-14).
proof_devices: LP relaxation of the lifting problem keeping only the lifted variable integral (eqs. (7)-(8), p. 5; Prop. 7, p. 9)
finite convergence via preservation of special-row properties for integer-coefficient cut families (Props. 11-12, pp. 15-16)
experiments: 50 Letchford-Lodi 0-1 multidimensional knapsacks, 50 self-generated general-integer knapsacks, MIPLIB p0033/p0040 from 20 starts; MGA with four lifting orders vs Glover and published IYA; % gap to CPLEX 10.1 optimum, cuts, time (pp. 16-25).
positioning: Revives the Young/Glover primal cutting-plane line and compares with Letchford-Lodi (2002), described as the best published primal results (pp. 2, 20).
writing: Each lifting-order variant is given an explicit motivation sentence (p. 19); conclusion lists five possible uses and four future directions (pp. 26-27).
limits_future: Larger study needed, especially with dual cutting planes; combine with Letchford-Lodi ideas; heuristics for which cuts/variables to strengthen; extend to continuous-variable coefficients (p. 27).

method_links.note: Gap measured against the CPLEX optimum in a hand-written textbook primal algorithm, but the IYA baseline is taken from published numbers, not rerun.
Multi-constraint information in place of single-row lifting, inside MILP.

transferable: Approximate an intractable lifting problem by keeping integrality only on the lifted variable, making each coefficient bound one LP (eqs. (7)-(8), p. 5).
Ablate an ordering rule with purpose-built arms: near-identical order (robustness), random order (does order matter), reversed order (is the chosen order poor) (p. 19).
Report the share of run time spent in the new component and the saving from warm starts (Table 4, p. 23).

quotes.text: Thus, approximately 97% of the cuts were improved using the algorithm of Section 2.
We also observe that MGA spends approximately 96% of the time in the lifting procedure.

title: Relations between facets of low- and high-dimensional group problems
contribution: Introduces the sequential-merge operator, which builds the first known facet families for general high-dimensional infinite group problems from lower-dimensional facets, with continuous coefficients not dominated by single-row cuts and cuts outside the first split closure, and studies the reverse projection to lower dimensions.
problem_entry: Computational studies suggest multi-row cuts and stronger continuous coefficients are more promising than new 1D facets; no facets known above dimension two and 1D tools do not generalise (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: g<>h: cut the last m rows in lifting space, add to the first row, apply a 1D cut (Def. 10, p. 8); facets merge into facets (Theorem 5, p. 14); row duplication with integer multipliers projects back to lower dimension (eq. (24), pp. 19-20; Theorem 6, p. 28).
assumptions: g, h continuous PL facet-defining with equality systems unique up to scaling and nondecreasing lifting-space representations (Theorem 5, p. 14).
proof_devices: Facet Theorem with equality sets, proved first on the spine S(g<>h) then everywhere (Def. 11 p. 12; Theorem 5 proof p. 14)
certify a cut is outside the rank-1 split closure by exhibiting a point of that closure cut off by it (Example 1, pp. 17-18)
non-extremality shown by phi = 1/2 phi1 + 1/2 phi2 (p. 20)
positioning: Builds on Gomory-Johnson and Johnson; relates to Dash-Gunluk two-step MIR and explains the three-gradient facets of Dey-Richard (S026) (p. 3).
writing: Opens with quotations from Aardal-Weismantel-Wolsey and Gomory-Johnson to legitimise higher-dimensional facets (pp. 2-3); flags the asymmetry of results as 'Surprisingly' (p. 3, p. 29).
limits_future: Necessity of conditions on h open (conjectured unnecessary, p. 16); projected merge fails even with GMICs (p. 20); all known high-dimensional facets derive from 1D ones; computational potential untested (p. 29).

method_links.note: Sufficiency theorem with a necessity proof for g, an explicit conjecture for h, and non-extreme counterexamples for the projection.
Same MILP multi-row programme as S026, motivated by computational studies.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: compose low-dimensional facets into high-dimensional ones
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Sequential-merge produces facets of PI(r, m+1) from facets of PI(r1,1) and PI(r2,m).

transferable: Give an abstract construction a tableau reading (cut rows, add to another row, cut again) so practitioners see it as a row operation (p. 8).
Show a cut is not a rank-1 split cut by exhibiting a point of the first split closure it separates (Example 1, pp. 17-18).

quotes.text: In fact, the result does not even necessarily hold when the constituent inequalities are GMICs.
we expect sequential-merge inequalities to also be successful in practice.

title: Composite lifting of group inequalities and an application to two-row mixing inequalities
contribution: Proposes composite lifting (lift one integer variable, then fill in) to strengthen non-minimal inequalities of the mixed integer infinite group relaxation, bounds the lifting problem and gives necessary conditions for minimality, and uses it to obtain a new class of extreme two-row mixing inequalities.
problem_entry: Sequential lifting is expensive and trivial fill-in may be weak; no paper asked what to do when trivial fill-in fails to give minimal inequalities (pp. 1, 6).
key_idea: Lift a single well-chosen integer variable x(a) via a modified lifting problem, then fill in (Section 3, p. 4); with a = (1 + r1/2 - r2/2, (r1+r2)/2) the strengthened two-row mixing function is extreme (Theorem 23, p. 17).
assumptions: pi extreme for the continuous relaxation (p. 2); phi PL, continuous, zero only at 0 (Theorem 8, p. 8); r1 + r2 <= 1 WLOG by negating rows (p. 13).
proof_devices: a-priori bound on the lifting multiplier n (Corollary 5, p. 7) replacing a roughly 350-case subadditivity check (pp. 5, 18)
necessary conditions for minimality used to choose a (Theorem 8, p. 8; pp. 5-6)
closed form for the lifted function so no lifting problem must be solved (p. 17)
experiments: none (informal trials over values of a, p. 5).
positioning: Combines sequential lifting and fill-in (Gomory-Johnson, Johnson, Balas-Jeroslow) and continues Dey-Wolsey on two-row lattice-free cuts; notes Dash-Gunluk's different mixing approach (pp. 1-2, 18).
writing: Section 4 opens by posing two explicit questions and saying where each is answered (p. 5); the abandoned proof route is reported with its cost (p. 5).
limits_future: Open whether a k-variable lifting sequence followed by fill-in can always produce a minimal function (p. 18).

method_links.note: Parameter choice guided by small numerical trials before proof, but trials not reported as data.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Bound on the lifting multiplier makes validity a short finite check instead of about 350 cases.

transferable: When a subadditivity proof explodes into hundreds of cases, bound the lifting problem's integer multiplier and prove validity through the bound (Corollary 5, p. 7; p. 18).
Filter candidate parameters with necessary conditions for minimality plus quick numerical trials before attempting a proof (Theorem 8; pp. 5-6).

quotes.text: This involved verification of approximately 350 different cases and the resulting proof was extremely tedious.
The lifting and fill-in process applied together in the composite lifting approach represents a compromise between the strength of inequalities and the difficulty in deriving them.

title: On the Chvátal-Gomory Closure of a Compact Convex Set
contribution: Proves that the Chvatal-Gomory closure of any compact convex set is a rational polytope, resolving Schrijver's open question for irrational polytopes and generalising the rational polytope, ellipsoid and strictly convex cases.
problem_entry: Open question in Schrijver's 1980 discussion section on irrational polytopes, plus convex IPs whose second-order cone sets have irrational generators (p. 2).
key_idea: Induction on dimension: lift CG cuts of exposed faces to K using the integer affine hull aff_I and Dirichlet approximation, build finite approximations agreeing with CC(K) on the relative boundary, then only finitely many cuts can cut a relative-interior vertex (pp. 3-4, 15-17).
assumptions: K non-empty, compact, convex (Theorem 2.1, p. 3); compactness justified because conv of integer points of a general convex set need not be polyhedral (footnote 2, p. 2).
proof_devices: Dirichlet simultaneous approximation to rotate CG cuts of a face into CG cuts of K (p. 4; Theorem 3.1, p. 6)
integer affine hull aff_I(A) = aff(aff(A) cap Z^n) (p. 3)
induction on affine dimension with a radius argument bounding the cuts that can separate relative-interior vertices (eq. (29), p. 17)
positioning: Generalises Chvatal-Schrijver and the authors' ellipsoid and strictly convex results [6, 7]; uses Schrijver's own boundary intersection idea (p. 2).
writing: Quotes the open question verbatim from Schrijver (p. 2) and gives a numbered proof outline mapped to sections before the lemmas (pp. 3-4).
limits_future: Non-compact convex sets set aside (footnote 2, p. 2); this preprint has no conclusion section.

method_links.note: A classical MILP closure theorem asked for convex integer programs (Method 3 step 1, 'Cutting plane closures ?').
Compactness hypothesis justified by why the result cannot hold without it.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Dirichlet's theorem handles irrational faces when lifting CG cuts.

transferable: When extending a polyhedral result to convex sets, name the new obstacle (irrationality) and find the classical tool that handles it (Dirichlet's theorem) (pp. 2-4).
Give a numbered proof outline mapped to sections before long technical lemmas (pp. 3-4).

quotes.text: The barrier in extending our understanding of the CG closure from the setting of the intersection of a strictly convex set and a rational polyhedra to the setting of a general convex set, is in dealing with irrationality.
New connections with diophantine approximations were necessary for the proof here.

title: On maximal S-free convex sets
contribution: Shows that maximal S-free convex sets are polyhedra with at most 2^dim(conv S) facets when S is the set of integer points of an arbitrary convex set, generalising Lovasz and Basu et al., and marks which rational-case properties fail in general.
problem_entry: Whether polyhedrality of maximal S-free sets (known for S from rational polyhedra) holds for S = P cap Z^n with P arbitrary convex; motivated by intersection-cut relaxations of mixed-integer convex sets such as SOC-representable ones (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Every S-free convex set lies in an S-free polyhedron, hyperplane or halfspace (Prop. 3.3, p. 4), proved by induction on dimension; facet count bounded by adapting Doignon-Bell-Scarf (Theorem 3.2, p. 4; Prop. 3.10, p. 10).
assumptions: S subset of Z^n with conv(S) cap Z^n = S (p. 1); affine subspace W (Theorem 3.1, p. 4); relaxed to finite unions of such S in Corollary 4.10 (pp. 14-15).
proof_devices: induction on dim W using Basu et al.'s affine-subspace theorem (Theorem 2.5, p. 3; pp. 4-5)
Doignon-Bell-Scarf bound adapted to facets without S-points in their relative interior (pp. 9-10)
Dirichlet property of strictly convex sets via Dirichlet's theorem (Prop. 4.9, p. 14)
positioning: Generalises Lovasz, Basu et al.; gives an alternative proof of Basu et al. that avoids rationality of conv(S) (p. 1).
writing: A closing Notes section lists differences from the rational case, each with a small explicit counterexample (pp. 11-15).
limits_future: Recession-direction symmetry fails in general (Example 4.2, p. 12) and holds under a Dirichlet property (p. 12); the facet bound fails for unions of S (hexagon, p. 15).

method_links.note: Lattice-free/intersection-cut theory from MILP asked for integer points in general convex sets, motivated by SOC-representable sets.
Each surviving property paired with a counterexample where the rational-case property fails and a sufficient condition restoring it.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Dirichlet property for strictly convex sets proved with Dirichlet's theorem.

transferable: After generalising a theorem, list which special-case properties survive and give a small explicit counterexample for each that does not (pp. 11-15).
Point out when the generalised proof yields a new proof of the special case avoiding its key hypothesis (p. 1).

quotes.text: This motivates the search for maximal S-free convex sets.
The following example shows that this result is not true in general.

title: A note on the split rank of intersection cuts
contribution: Gives the first general lower bound on the split rank of intersection cuts, ceil(log2 l) for l tight integer points on distinct facets of a restricted lattice-free set, and derives ceil(log2(n+1)) for n-row mixing and lot-sizing inequalities.
problem_entry: Split cuts are among the most successful general cuts, so compare other classes by split rank; no general technique for lower bounds existed (pp. 2, 4).
key_idea: Build the restricted lattice-free set Q~ inside the lattice-free set (Def. 3, p. 6) and count integer points on distinct facets: split rank >= ceil(log2 l) (Theorem 1, p. 11); mixing inequalities as an application (Prop. 3, p. 14).
assumptions: Corner relaxation x = f + sum r^i y_i, x integer, y >= 0, rational data, f non-integral (p. 2); a mild column condition stated as Assumption 1 (pp. 2, 5).
proof_devices: halving induction: each split disjunction partitions the tight points into two sides, so more than 2^t points keep gamma^{I,w,t} > 0 (Theorem 1 proof, pp. 11-12)
base case from the dimension of Q~ (Prop. 2, p. 10)
positioning: Contrasts with known upper bounds (Balas, Nemhauser-Wolsey, Dash-Gunluk) and infinite-rank examples (Cook-Kannan-Schrijver, Li-Richard) (pp. 3-4).
writing: Short note; discussion section states where the bound is weak and gives the competing infinite-rank result (pp. 16-17).
limits_future: Bound weak when Q~ has integral vertices and integer points in every facet (Li-Richard simplex: infinite rank vs ceil(log2(m+1))); open whether split rank depends only on Q~ (pp. 16-17).

method_links.note: Names the regime where its own bound is weak, with the instance and the true (infinite) rank.
Measure chosen because split cuts work in practice, but the question is comparative, not an explanation of a solver habit.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: halving argument for closure-rank lower bounds
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Tight integer points on distinct facets force ceil(log2 l) split rounds.

transferable: Lower-bound a closure rank by finding many tight integer points on distinct facets and arguing each disjunction splits them into only two groups (pp. 11-12).
In the discussion, place the family where your bound is weakest next to the strongest known bound for it (pp. 16-17).

quotes.text: To the best of our knowledge there are no known general techniques to obtain lower bounds on the split rank of valid inequalities for mixed integer programs.

Therefore, if the lower bound on the split rank of an inequality is high, it may be better to apply this inequality directly to the linear programming (LP) relaxation of the problem instead of generating it using a sequence of split cuts.

title: On mixed-integer sets with two integer variables
contribution: Shows that every facet of a polyhedral mixed-integer set with two integer variables (or a rank-2 integer coefficient matrix) is a crooked cross cut, characterises the CC closure in Cook-Kannan-Schrijver style (implying dominance over 2-branch split cuts), and extends the results to compact convex relaxations.
problem_entry: Generalise the authors' 2010 two-variable, two-constraint result to arbitrary constraints, rank-2 matrices and convex relaxations (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: The region removed by a valid inequality projects to a lattice-free set in R^2, which lies inside a CC set, so the inequality is a CC cut (Lemma 2.1, pp. 2-3); CC closure equals intersection of conv{P^LP : pi1 x, pi2 x integral} (Theorem 3.1, pp. 3-5); unimodular reduction for rank 2 (Theorem 4.1, pp. 5-6).
assumptions: Rational polyhedral P with Ax + Gy = b, y >= 0 (p. 1); closed bounded convex C in Section 5 (p. 6).
proof_devices: rational description of projections with strict inequalities (Lemma A.1 via Motzkin transposition, pp. 8-9) and integer rounding px < q+1 to get a closed lattice-free set (p. 3)
auxiliary integer variables z = pi x to transfer the two-variable result to closures (Theorem 3.1, pp. 4-5)
unimodular column transformation reducing rank-2 A to two integer variables (Theorem 4.1, pp. 5-6)
strict separation plus finitely many integer points in a bounding polytope for compact convex C (Theorem 5.1, pp. 6-7)
positioning: Parallels Cook-Kannan-Schrijver's alternative split-cut definition; settles dominance over Li-Richard 2-branch split cuts; relates to Eisenbrand et al. and Andersen-Louveaux-Weismantel (pp. 3, 5, 8).
writing: Short letter with all results summarised at the end of the introduction (p. 2) and explicit contrasts between polyhedral and convex versions (p. 7).
limits_future: For compact convex C only strictly valid inequalities are shown to be CC cuts (p. 7); open whether 2D lattice-free cuts give conv(P) for n1 = 2, m > 2, and whether rank-2 split cuts exist that are not CC cuts (p. 3).

method_links.note: MILP closure characterisation and convex-hull result carried to mixed-integer sets in a compact convex set.
States exactly where the convex result is weaker than the polyhedral one and lists open cases.

transferable: To show a valid inequality belongs to a cut class, project the removed region to a lattice-free set and embed it in the class's lattice-free template (Lemma 2.1, pp. 2-3).
Prove a closure equals an intersection of convex hulls by adding auxiliary integer variables z = pi x and applying the small-dimension result (Theorem 3.1, pp. 4-5).

quotes.text: We are not able to simply reuse the proof of Lemma 2.1 as there we explicitly use the polyhedrality of P
This result is in contrast to Lemma 2.1, where every facet-defining inequality for conv (P) is a CC cut.
